newsitem.title: USA: Dlr consolidates, closes little changed in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dlr consolidates, closes little changed in U.S..

text.p: The dollar ended little changed on Tuesday as traders booked profits one day after a rally that boosted the U.S. unit to a 32-month high, experts said.
However, the dollar's outlook remained decidedly positive, with further gains expected down the road, they said.

"I think that the market was prone to some profit-taking given the kind of large run-up we've seen in the dollar over the last few days," said Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in New York.
The dollar had soared briefly to 111.68 yen on Monday, its highest level since hitting 111.75 yen in January 1994.
The dollar closed at 111.40/47 yen and 1.5259/66 marks, slightly higher than 111.23/28 yen and 1.5245/50 marks at the open.
Speculation that the dollar could rally further circulated in the market.
"The thing about the dollar's consolidation right here is that it's happening at higher levels," said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International.
"I think that's probably encouraging people, making them think -- alright there's probably some room on the upside here," he said.

News that the United States and Japan have agreed to try to settle a long-running dispute over the insurance market in Japan by the end of this year also gave the dollar a psychological lift. Acting U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky made the announcement on Tuesday.
"It's mildly supportive but I'd say that it's had very little direct impact on the exchange rate," Lynch said.

Denial of remarks by a key Japanese financial official and comments from the head of the powerful Japan Federation of Economic Organizations or Keidanren had briefly pressured the dollar during the Asian session, experts said.

A Japanese news agency on Tuesday quoted Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the international finance bureau of Japan's Ministry of Finance, as telling an American economist Japan would not raise interest rates at least until the end of the current fiscal year that closes on March 31.
Yet Sakakibara denied making the remarks.
"The implication is that they might raise rates before the end of the fiscal year which would be negative for the dollar," said Chris Iggo, an international economist at Barclays Bank Plc.

Keidanren Chairman Shoichiro Toyoda also reportedly told a press conference on Tuesday that exchange rates of 100 to 110 yen to the dollar are broadly in line with Japanese economic fundamentals and 111 yen per dollar is within acceptable bounds, although the level is slightly weak for the Japanese currency.
The dollar, however, managed to erase overnight declines in New York as a positive outlook prevailed.
In other trade, the dollar finished at 1.2552/59 Swiss francs, up from 1.2533/38 francs at the opening.
Sterling finished at $1.5643/50, up from $1.5637/42 at the opening.
The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3590/95, down from C$1.3626/31 at the opening.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7913/18.
-- Donna Sells, 212-859-1668
